title: Rectangular, polar and phasors
blurb: Plot impedances in rectangular form, convert to polar, and read phasor diagrams and the E5-1 figure.

E5C01.why: Capacitive reactance is negative j and there is no resistance: **0 − j100**.
E5C01.trap: +j is inductive; the real part (first number) is resistance.

E5C02.why: Polar form gives a **magnitude and a phase angle**, e.g. 50 Ω ∠30°.
E5C02.trap: R and X, or real and imaginary parts, describe rectangular form.

E5C03.why: A pure inductive reactance points straight up on the plane: **+90°**.
E5C03.trap: −90° is capacitive; ±45° needs equal R and X.

E5C04.why: Responses span huge ranges, so graphs use a **logarithmic** vertical scale, often in dB.

E5C05.why: A **phasor diagram** shows the phase relationship between voltages, currents or impedances at one frequency.

E5C06.why: In R ± jX the first number is resistance (50 Ω) and −j25 is **25 Ω of capacitive reactance**, in series.

E5C07.why: Pure resistance has X = 0, so it plots **on the horizontal axis**.

E5C08.why: **Polar coordinates** (magnitude and angle) show the phase angle of R, L and C circuits.
E5C08.trap: A Maidenhead grid locates stations on Earth.

E5C09.why: Horizontal axis = resistance (R); vertical axis = reactance (X).
E5C09.trap: Phase angle and magnitude are the polar quantities, not the rectangular axes.

E5C12.trap: An inductor would be above the axis; a capacitor is below.
